sourceBindings.text: Use the three jars you prepared in the previous step only after their final observation is recorded. Measure each mineral layer, calculate a labelled classroom estimate, and trace the three percentages on a soil texture triangle. A worked jar or a calculator can teach the method, but it cannot replace your own measurements.

Measure the separate sand, silt and clay layer thicknesses and total mineral-layer height in millimetres for three traceable samples, distinguishing a mark's cumulative height from the thickness between marks.
Calculate each approximate jar-layer percentage using the total mineral-layer height, find a missing layer or percentage from a complete balance, and explain the rounding check.
Trace sand, silt and clay lines on the labelled USDA texture triangle and justify the class of worked cases, including 55/30/15 as sandy loam; use a calculator as a check after explaining the trace.

sourceBindings.text: Cumulative marks are at 44, 68 and 80 mm from the bottom.
Separate thicknesses are 44, 24 and 12 mm, not 44, 68 and 80 mm.
Divide each thickness by 80 mm: 55% sand, 30% silt, 15% clay; both height and percent totals balance.
Trace 55 sand and 15 clay, confirm 30 silt: the USDA texture class at this point is sandy loam.
Measure the thicknesses, calculate their percentages, then trace the class.

sourceBindings.text: A 100 mm example has 25 mm sand and 45 mm silt. The clay height is missing.
The three mineral layer thicknesses sum to the 100 mm total.
Clay percentage = 30 mm ÷ 100 mm × 100 = 30%.
Find the missing thickness before computing or choosing the percentage.

units.scientificMeaning:
A 100 mm example has 25 mm sand and 45 mm silt. The clay height is missing.

The three mineral layer thicknesses sum to the 100 mm total.

Clay = 100 − 25 − 45 = 30 mm.

Clay percentage = 30 mm ÷ 100 mm × 100 = 30%.

Find the missing thickness before computing or choosing the percentage.

units.spokenText:
An example with a total height of one hundred millimetres has twenty-five millimetres sand and forty-five millimetres silt. The clay height is missing.

The three mineral layer thicknesses sum to the one hundred millimetres total.

Clay equals one hundred minus twenty-five minus forty-five equals thirty millimetres.

Clay percentage equals thirty millimetres divided by one hundred millimetres multiplied by one hundred equals thirty percent.

Find the missing thickness before computing or choosing the percentage.

sourceBindings.text: The class traces 30% sand, 30% silt and 40% clay together on the printed USDA triangle.
The values total 100%.
Find the 40% clay line and 30% sand line; confirm 30% silt.
The standard chart places this point on the clay-region threshold. Mark it on the actual chart and discuss the boundary instead of guessing from the word 'clay'.
A boundary point needs careful line tracing and an identified chart convention.

Because each total is 100 mm, the layer heights have the same numeric value as their approximate jar percentages.

Practice data support reasoning, not a claim of personal performance.

sourceBindings.text: On an accessible 3D teaching jar, drag three horizontal boundary markers to 44, 68 and 80 mm, enter separate thicknesses and calculate 55/30/15 with visible feedback. Then trace those percentages on an editable USDA triangle, correct the reversed-label distractor, practise the 30/30/40 boundary and sort the supplied A/B/C model rows. A distinct blank record is reserved for real supervised measurements.
The online simulation rehearses reasoning; only observation of each learner measuring three identified real jars can pass C01.

sourceBindings.text: cumulative height
Distance from the same bottom reference to a boundary mark; not automatically the thickness of the layer above an earlier mark.
layer thickness
Distance between the lower and upper boundary of one settled mineral layer.
total mineral-layer height
Distance from the bottom to the final settled clay boundary, excluding floating organic material.
jar-height percentage
One observed mineral-layer thickness divided by total observed mineral-layer height ×100; an approximate classroom estimate.
USDA texture triangle
A chart locating a mineral soil textural class from the relative sand, silt and clay percentages of the fine-earth fraction.
sandy loam
The USDA texture region containing the 55% sand, 30% silt and 15% clay worked point.
